recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A soft blue haze spreads among countless galaxies in the cluster Abell S1063, about 4 billion light-years away in the constellation Grus. The haze is intracluster light, the glow of stars that have been thrown out of their galaxies.

Those stars no longer belong to any galaxy. Torn loose during interactions between galaxies, they now follow the gravity of the cluster as a whole, the same gravity that governs the cluster's invisible dark matter. Because they trace the same pull, the faint glow works as a map of where the dark matter lies.

A study using Hubble Frontier Fields images of six massive galaxy clusters found that intracluster light matched the clusters' mass maps better than X-ray emission did. The method needs only deep imaging rather than slower spectroscopy, so many more clusters could be studied in less time. In the original Frontier Fields work, the glow was a nuisance that partly hid distant galaxies behind the clusters.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras in visible and near-infrared light. NASA shows F435W and F606W in blue, F814W and F105W in green, and F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Intracluster light is a faint glow that Hubble's sensitivity picks out, and part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

explore: Mireia Montes (University of New South Wales) and Ignacio Trujillo (Canary Islands Institute of Astronomy) carried out the work. They compared shapes using a measure called the Modified Hausdorff Distance. Trujillo hoped to try the same approach on single galaxies, using the stars in their halos.
